subject: English
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 50 minutes × 7 periods = 350 minutes
Total: 7 periods · 5h 50min

periods.activity_title: Entering the Poem — Pre-Reading and First Read-Aloud

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.220): pre-reading discussion — can we communicate without words?
Reflect and Respond (p.220): word-grid activity — find and fill seven vocabulary words from the poem.

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with the Reflect and Respond oral prompt: why are words important, and can we communicate without them? Students share responses briefly in pairs before reporting to the class.
Teacher reads the poem aloud expressively while students follow in their textbooks; teacher then invites two or three students to read individual stanzas aloud, observing the poem's hymn-like rhythm.

Students work on the word-grid puzzle from Reflect and Respond (p.220), finding all seven horizontal and vertical vocabulary items; teacher circulates, confirms answers on the board, and discusses each word's meaning in the context of the poem.

periods.teacher_notes: The poem's ABAB rhyme scheme and iambic metre give it a hymn-like quality — draw attention to this during the read-aloud so students feel the rhythm before analysing it. The word-grid words (depart, weeds, impart, pilgrim, feast, blossom, satisfy) all recur as key poetic terms, so getting them right here prepays the device-analysis work ahead. Students who finish the grid early may be asked to locate each word in the poem and note the stanza.
materials: Textbook p.220–224 (poem text and Reflect and Respond word grid)

periods.activity_title: Comprehension Check — Poem Summary and Rhyme Scheme

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.222): fill-in-the-blank paragraph summarising the poem's ideas.
Reading for Appreciation (p.222–223): identify four rhyming-word sets and write the rhyme scheme.

time_bands.activity: Teacher leads a brisk whole-class oral recap of the poem's central argument — that sincere, few words outweigh a torrent of hollow ones — before students individually complete the fill-in-the-blank summary paragraph from Check Your Understanding (p.222).

Students compare answers in pairs; teacher projects or writes the seven blanks on the board and confirms the correct words (depart, pilgrim, weeds, joy, lonely, world, fruit), connecting each to the stanza it appears in.

Class moves to the rhyme scheme task from Reading for Appreciation (p.222–223): students identify four sets of rhyming words (e.g. heart/depart, care/air, earth/worth, needs/weeds) and confirm the ABAB pattern; teacher then reads one stanza aloud to demonstrate the metre before students mark stressed syllables in their books.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often confuse rhyme scheme labelling — spend a moment showing that each new end-sound gets a new letter, and that ABAB means alternate rhyme, not couplets. Having read the poem aloud previously, students should recognise the sounds more readily; tie the metre discussion to the 'hymn-like' quality noted earlier. Students who confuse 'pilgrim' as a religious term alone should be redirected to its metaphorical use — the heart as a restless wanderer seeking connection.
materials: Textbook p.222–223 (Check Your Understanding and Reading for Appreciation)

periods.activity_title: Poetic Devices — Simile, Metaphor, Hyperbole, Repetition

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.223): identify poetic devices and explain their purpose in phrases (i)–(iv).
Reading for Appreciation (p.223): identify poetic devices and explain their purpose in phrases (v)–(vii).
Reading for Appreciation (p.223): identify repeated words and explain why the poet uses repetition.

homework.task_brief: Reading for Appreciation (p.223–224): identify hyperbole example and complete four paired hyperbole sentences.

time_bands.activity: Teacher briefly recaps the three core similes from the poem — words like summer birds, words like weeds, words like gaudy plants — asking students to locate each stanza; this sets the frame for the device-identification work.

Students work in pairs on phrases (i)–(iv) from Reading for Appreciation (p.223): they name the device (simile, metaphor) and write a sentence explaining the poet's purpose; pairs share findings and teacher clarifies the distinction between simile and metaphor using the 'heart as pilgrim' example.

Class tackles phrases (v)–(vii) — the feast metaphor and the gaudy-plant simile — followed by the repetition question; teacher draws a table on the board listing the repeated phrase 'satisfy' and 'words' and asks students to articulate how repetition reinforces the poem's central paradox.

periods.teacher_notes: The gaudy-plant simile (phrases vi–vii) trips students who read 'all blossom to the root' as praise; guide them to see that showy blossom with no fruit is the critique — empty words look impressive but yield nothing. The stanza-ending exclamation marks (task 7 in the textbook, left unanchored here) are a useful doorway into the device discussion; a brief mention — 'notice how the exclamation sharpens the disillusionment' — costs little and enriches the analysis. Hyperbole and the exclamation-mark MCQ are assigned for home reinforcement.
materials: Textbook p.223–224 (Reading for Appreciation, phrases i–vii, and repetition prompt)

periods.activity_title: Critical Reflection on Extracts and Figurative-Phrase Matching

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.224–225): five close-reading questions on the 'pilgrim' extract — motivation, emotion, and nature of communication.
Vocabulary in Context (p.226): match six figurative phrases from the poem to their meanings; write one sentence per phrase.

time_bands.activity: Students read the 'pilgrim' stanza silently (directed to the locator: stanza 2, p.221) before tackling all five questions from Critical Reflection (p.224–225) individually; teacher then leads a whole-class debrief, pressing for textual evidence on the emotions the heart experiences and the nature of communication question.

Class moves to the figurative-phrase matching task from Vocabulary in Context (p.226): teacher displays the six phrases on the board, students match them in pairs, then each pair chooses two phrases and reads their original sentences aloud; teacher confirms or corrects meaning and register.

periods.teacher_notes: Rule 2 Step 4 requires vocabulary_grammar to have its own period slot, but since the vocabulary task here is a single matching exercise that fits comfortably alongside the close-reading work, it is placed as the second spine in this unit to keep the schedule honest; if time is short, the sentence-writing part of the matching task can be completed individually at home. Students frequently confuse 'wins its sunny way' as a weather metaphor — redirect them to the poem's claim that a warm, cheerful voice needs few words. The critical reflection's final ECR question on the nature of communication should be treated as an extended written response, not an oral one.
materials: Textbook p.221 (stanza 2 'pilgrim' locator), p.224–225 (Critical Reflection), p.226 (Vocabulary in Context matching task)

periods.activity_title: Listening to Communication Conversation and Quotation Presentations

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.227): mark four true statements from six after listening to the Sonali–Vivek conversation.
Speaking Activity (p.227): choose one quotation, explain it, share a personal connection, and use the given verbal cue phrases.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the transcript of the Sonali–Vivek conversation aloud twice at a natural pace (Listen and Respond, p.227); students listen the first time with books closed, then on the second reading mark their four true statements from the six provided before comparing with a partner.

Teacher confirms the four correct statements with brief reasoning drawn from the transcript — body language, vocabulary, confidence, and the library reference section — addressing any statements students found ambiguous.

Students individually select one quotation from the Speaking Activity (p.227) and deliver a short oral presentation using the verbal cue phrases ('I chose… because…'); teacher ensures at least four or five students present, noting effective use of evidence and personal connection.

periods.teacher_notes: The transcript's key claims — that communication needs well-organised thoughts, appropriate vocabulary, and body language — echo the poem's argument that quality of expression matters more than quantity; a brief bridging comment before the listening task helps students hear the thematic continuity. For the speaking task, the verbal cues printed in the textbook are scaffolds, not scripts — discourage students from reading them verbatim. Students who did not yet read the quotations may scan them in the first minute of the speaking segment.
materials: Textbook p.227 (Listen and Respond statements and Speaking Activity quotations)
Transcript text: Sonali and Vivek conversation (Unit 7, p.273)

periods.activity_title: Structured Essay — Drafting and Peer Response

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.228): plan and draft a five-paragraph argumentative essay on a chosen quotation, following the provided structural guidelines.

time_bands.activity: Teacher models the essay structure on the board — introduction (quotation + purpose), two body paragraphs (topic sentence → evidence → transition), counterargument, conclusion — using a short exemplar opening sentence to demonstrate register and stance.

Students plan their essay (quotation choice, main claim, two supporting points, counterargument) in a brief outline, then begin drafting; teacher circulates and offers targeted guidance on introductions and the counterargument paragraph, which students consistently find difficult.

Students swap drafts with a partner for a quick peer response: the reader identifies whether the introduction names the quotation and states a purpose, whether each body paragraph has a topic sentence, and whether the counterargument is present; writers note feedback and complete or revise their draft within the remaining time.

periods.teacher_notes: The counterargument paragraph is the weakest point for most students — model one possible objection to the chosen quotation (e.g. 'one might argue that words alone cannot change circumstances') before students draft independently. Because the oral presentations in the previous part of the chapter gave students a chance to articulate their chosen quotation's meaning, they should have a working argument ready; encourage them to draw on what they said aloud. Finished drafts should be complete within this unit — do not plan for further revision outside this sitting.
materials: Textbook p.228 (Writing Task guidelines and essay structure)
Blank paper or exercise books for drafting

periods.activity_title: Non-Verbal Communication Games and Comparative Poem Reading

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Learning Beyond the Text (p.229): play the Non-verbal game in groups of six — enact emotion/gesture slips and score points for two rounds.
Learning Beyond the Text (p.229): read about Charles-Michel de l'Épée and discuss sign language as a form of non-verbal communication.
Learning Beyond the Text (p.229–230): read 'Weigh Your Words' by E. F. Hayward and discuss thematic parallels with Swain's poem.

time_bands.activity: Students form groups of six and play the Non-verbal game from Learning Beyond the Text (p.229): each student writes an emotion emoji on one slip and a gesture on another, slips are shuffled, and each player enacts their draw in thirty seconds while the group identifies it; the two-round scoring finds the Non-verbal Champion.

Teacher shares the brief passage about Charles-Michel de l'Épée from Learning Beyond the Text (p.229) and leads a short discussion: how does sign language demonstrate that meaningful communication transcends spoken words — a theme directly echoed in Swain's argument that few sincere words outweigh many hollow ones.

Students read 'Weigh Your Words' by E. F. Hayward (p.229–230) silently, then in a brief paired exchange identify one similarity and one difference in theme or tone between Hayward's poem and Swain's 'Words'; pairs share findings in a quick whole-class round.

periods.teacher_notes: The non-verbal game works best with pre-written slips — allow two minutes at the start for students to write their slips before grouping them. The connection between de l'Épée's work and the poem's theme (communication beyond words) is a rich interdisciplinary moment; invite students who know any Indian Sign Language signs to demonstrate. The Hayward poem comparison is an accessible comparative-reading task: students will likely notice both poets value quality over quantity of words, but Hayward stresses moral consequence whereas Swain focuses on emotional inadequacy.
materials: Textbook p.229–230 (Non-verbal game instructions, de l'Épée passage, 'Weigh Your Words' poem)
Small slips of paper and pens for the Non-verbal game

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, tone, and the poet's argument about language using a lyric poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Swain's paradox that sincere, few words outweigh a torrent of hollow speech, through simile, metaphor, and hymn-like metre.
items.item_stem: Read the third stanza of the poem on p.221, beginning “A little said, and truly said.” Which of the following best states the claim Swain makes in this stanza?

options.label: A
options.text: A few sincere words bring more joy than a large quantity of empty ones.

options.label: B
options.text: Joy comes from repeating words until they feel meaningful.

options.label: C
options.text: Saying very little is always better than saying a great deal.

options.label: D
options.text: Words that reach the head are always more valuable than words that touch the heart.

what_each_option_reveals.C: Confuses 'a little said' with a blanket endorsement of silence; misses the qualifier 'and truly said'.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Inverts the poem's hierarchy — Swain explicitly says words that only reach the head without touching the heart are of lesser worth.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Invents a notion of repetition not present in this stanza; confuses the device of repetition elsewhere with the poem's argument here.

items.source_lo: Student analyses poetic devices, tone, and the poet's argument about language using a lyric poem as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Swain's paradox that sincere, few words outweigh a torrent of hollow speech, through simile, metaphor, and hymn-like metre.
items.item_stem:
Read the final stanza on p.221, beginning “Like plants that make a gaudy show.”

1. Identify the poetic device in these lines and name its two terms of comparison.
2. Explain what the poet communicates about hollow words through this image.
3. How does the tone of this stanza differ from the tone of the first stanza? Support your answer with evidence from both stanzas.
items.visual_stimulus: Read the final stanza on p.221, beginning “Like plants that make a gaudy show.”

expected_elements: Identifies the device as simile; terms are hollow words and gaudy plants.
Explains that showy blossom without fruit images words that look impressive but yield nothing.
Contrasts the first stanza's wistful disappointment with the final stanza's sharper frustration or contempt.
Cites evidence: first stanza uses 'depart and leave but empty air'; final stanza uses 'poor nature cannot grow one particle of fruit'.
Notes the exclamation mark in the final stanza intensifies the critical tone.

items.source_lo: Student listens critically to a spoken conversation and identifies accurate information by distinguishing true statements from false ones.
items.source_context: Sonali and Vivek's conversation on English communication, vocabulary, grammar, and the role of body language.
items.item_stem: Listen to the conversation between Sonali and Vivek. Decide whether each statement below is True or False.

options.text: According to Sonali, insufficient vocabulary and grammar knowledge causes hesitation in communication.
Sonali registered for the declamation contest before Vivek did.
Sonali tells Vivek that body language plays no significant role in communication.
Vivek believes the contest topic is unsuitable for discussion.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1 — True: Sonali confirms she registered early. 2 — False: Vivek adds positively to the topic discussion. 3 — True: Sonali explicitly states this. 4 — False: Sonali says body language is important and must be worked on.

items.source_lo: Student listens critically to a spoken conversation and identifies accurate information by distinguishing true statements from false ones.
items.source_context: Sonali and Vivek's conversation on English communication, vocabulary, grammar, and the role of body language.
items.item_stem: In the conversation, Sonali makes two separate recommendations to help someone communicate confidently in English. In two or three sentences, state both recommendations and explain why, according to Sonali, body language is relevant alongside vocabulary and grammar.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Sonali recommends developing vocabulary and grammar to build confidence, and working on body language — gestures and postures — because communication happens not only through words but also through physical expression. Body language is relevant because it visibly reflects a speaker's confidence, so improving it reinforces the verbal message.

items.item_stem: Choose one of the quotations you have read in this chapter. In a short spoken presentation, describe what the quotation means, explain why you chose it using at least one of the verbal cue phrases ('I chose… because…'; 'I selected… since…'; 'I settled for… because…'), and share a brief personal experience that connects to its message.

expected_elements: Clearly states the quotation and identifies the speaker.
Explains the quotation's meaning in own words accurately.
Uses at least one verbal cue phrase correctly and naturally.
Links the quotation to a specific personal experience or observation.
Speaks audibly and coherently without reading from the textbook.

items.item_stem: A classmate argues: 'Inspirational quotations are just nice-sounding phrases — they don't actually change how people behave.' Do you agree or disagree? Present your position in a short oral argument, giving at least two reasons supported by evidence from the poem 'Words' or the quotations discussed in class, and acknowledge the opposing view before concluding.

expected_elements: States a clear position (agree or disagree) at the outset.
Gives at least two reasons grounded in the poem or a quotation from class.
Acknowledges the opposing view fairly before refuting or qualifying it.
Uses appropriate discourse markers (however, in contrast, therefore).
Concludes with a restatement of position and a lasting thought.

items.source_context: Essay arguing the significance of mindful speech, inspired by the themes of quality versus quantity of words in the chapter.
items.item_stem: Your school magazine has invited students to submit a short article for its 'Young Voices' column. Write an article (around 150 words) addressed to fellow students, explaining why the quality of what we say matters more than how much we say. Use at least one concrete example from everyday life to support your point.

expected_elements: Opens with an engaging hook — a question, anecdote, or observation.
States a clear central claim about quality over quantity of words.
Supports the claim with at least one concrete everyday example.
Uses magazine-article register: second person, accessible tone, short paragraphs.
Concludes with a memorable call to action or reflective sentence.

items.source_lo: Student plans and drafts a structured argumentative essay using evidence, counterargument, and a concluding judgement.
items.source_context: Essay arguing the significance of mindful speech, inspired by the themes of quality versus quantity of words in the chapter.
items.item_stem: Write a structured five-paragraph argumentative essay on the following proposition: 'In the age of social media, we speak more but communicate less.' Your essay must include an introduction that states your position, two body paragraphs each built around a distinct argument with supporting evidence, a counterargument paragraph that identifies and refutes a possible objection, and a conclusion that summarises your reasoning and ends with a lasting judgement.

expected_elements: Introduction names the proposition and states a clear position.
Each body paragraph opens with a topic sentence and provides evidence or reasoning.
Counterargument paragraph fairly presents an objection before refuting it.
Uses formal essay register with appropriate discourse markers (furthermore, however, nevertheless).
Conclusion restates position and ends with a substantive, non-trivial judgement.

items.item_stem: Match each figurative phrase from the poem in Column A with its correct meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
| Column A | Column B |
|---|---|
| 1. hosts of words | a. to comfort and brighten a sad or lonely place |
| 2. never touch the heart | b. a great many words spoken or written |
| 3. wins its sunny way | c. things that appear impressive but produce no real value |
| 4. plants that cannot grow fruit | d. to fail to reach someone emotionally |
| 5. depart and leave but empty air | e. to go away leaving nothing meaningful behind |

answer_key.right: a great many words spoken or written
to fail to reach someone emotionally
to comfort and brighten a sad or lonely place
things that appear impressive but produce no real value

answer_key.left: depart and leave but empty air
answer_key.right: to go away leaving nothing meaningful behind

items.source_lo: Student interprets figurative language in context by matching poetic phrases to their meanings and using them in original sentences.
items.source_context: Six figurative phrases from Swain's poem — including 'hosts of words', 'heart a pilgrim', and 'plants that cannot grow fruit'.
items.item_stem: Use any three of the figurative phrases from the poem — 'hosts of words', 'never touch the heart', 'wins its sunny way', 'plants that cannot grow fruit', 'depart and leave but empty air' — in three separate original sentences. Each sentence must show that you understand the phrase's figurative meaning, not its literal one. Then, for one of your three sentences, explain in a further sentence why the phrase is more expressive than a plain, literal equivalent would be.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Accept any three well-formed sentences that use the phrases figuratively (e.g. 'Despite her hosts of words of apology, his hurt remained'). The explanatory sentence should identify what the figurative phrase adds — emotional weight, vividness, or brevity — over a plain restatement.

items.source_lo: Student explores non-verbal and cross-cultural communication forms and compares thematic concerns across two poems.
items.source_context: Non-verbal game, de l'Épée's contribution to sign language, and a comparative reading of Hayward's 'Weigh Your Words'.
items.item_stem: Charles-Michel de l'Épée developed a systematic sign language to enable deaf individuals to communicate. In a short paragraph of four to five sentences, explain how de l'Épée's work supports the idea that meaningful communication does not depend on spoken words alone. Connect your answer to at least one idea from Swain's poem 'Words'.

expected_elements: Identifies de l'Épée as a pioneer of sign language for deaf education.
Explains that sign language demonstrates communication can be non-verbal and fully meaningful.
Links this to Swain's argument that quality and sincerity matter more than spoken quantity.
Uses at least one specific image or phrase from the poem to support the connection.
Writes in coherent paragraph form with a clear topic sentence.

items.source_lo: Student explores non-verbal and cross-cultural communication forms and compares thematic concerns across two poems.
items.source_context: Non-verbal game, de l'Épée's contribution to sign language, and a comparative reading of Hayward's 'Weigh Your Words'.
items.item_stem: Both Charles Swain's 'Words' and E. F. Hayward's 'Weigh Your Words' are concerned with how people use language. Design a short project comparing the two poems. Your project must: (a) identify one theme that both poems share; (b) identify one way in which their concerns differ; (c) find one poetic device used in each poem and explain what it contributes; and (d) conclude with your view on which poem makes the stronger argument about the use of words, and why. Present your project as a written response of around 200 words.

expected_elements: Identifies a shared theme, e.g. the moral or emotional weight of careless speech.
Notes a clear difference: Swain focuses on emotional inadequacy; Hayward on moral consequence and conscience.
Names a device from each poem (e.g. Swain's simile 'words like summer birds'; Hayward's metaphor 'written on a heart') and explains its effect.
Presents a reasoned personal judgement on which poem argues more effectively, supported by textual evidence.
Organises the response clearly with each of the four required points addressed.
